# Bird sexes

- Two sexes: M/F (c.f. hermaphrodites, clonal reproduction, animals with 4-7 mating types)
- Sex is determined at fertilization, permanent (c.f. some fish, frogs, reptiles)
- Roles and phenotypes determined by gene activity, hormones, **chromosomes**

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/bop_sexes.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Paradisaea apoda*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/225439061))

# ZW sex determination

- Females are the **heterogametic** sex

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/bird_sex_chrom.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Bird reproductive organs

- Most female birds only have one ovary, on the left side (excluding kiwis, raptors)
- More germ cells on left side in male birds leads to large L testis
- Produce **testosterone** and **estrogen** (both sexes have both; ratio matters)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/bird_genitals.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Sexual dimorphism is not ubiquitous 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/empid_sex.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Empidonax difficilis*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/642411374))  

# Sexual differences are not absolute

- Failure during first mitotic division of fertilized ovum leads to **bilateral gynandromorphs** with one testis / one ovum, M/F halves

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.4\linewidth]{images/gynandromorph.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Agate et al. 2003)  

# Bilateral gynandromorphs are not uncommon

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/gynandromorph2.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.discoverwildlife.com/news/bilateral-gynandromorphy-in-green-honeycreeper

# Copulation via cloacal contact

- accumulating sperm produces **cloacal protrubrence** in some passerines; can indicate reproductive status  

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/cp.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Pyle 1997; Schut et al. 2012)  

# Ratites and waterfowl retain a penis

- Universal in reptiles and mammals, lost in all other birds
- Erections from lymphatic fluids, not blood pressure
- Retained within body until explosive activation 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/ruddy_duck_dick.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (McCracken et al. 2003)  

# Sperm production

- Sperm produced at night during cooler temperatures
- Stored at distal end of vas deferens (4 degrees C cooler than body)
- Sperm morphology and size vary widely across birds---even within passerines

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/sperm.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019; [NHM U. Oslo](https://www.nhm.uio.no/english/research/projects/sperm-evolution-in-birds/))  

# Ova maturation

- Oocytes present at hatching
- Ova by two months of age
- Add yolk in week prior to ovulation 
- **L**: dissected female House Sparrow that had previously laid 4 eggs; a fifth is visible in the oviduct, plus two more forming yolk 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/ova.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019; photo courtesy Jay Rotella)

\normalsize

a) males have ZZ chromosomes
b) kiwis have paired ovaries
c) females have a cloaca
d) not all birds are sexually dimorphic
e) the right male testis is largest

# Ovulation

- Egg moves through oviduct in ~24 hours (albumen, 3-4 hours; egg membranes, 1 hour; shell, 20 hours)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/ovulation.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Egg anatomy 

- yellow yolk deposited at night, white during the day
- **carotenoids** determine yolk color
- yolk for food (21-36% lipids, 16-22% proteins)
- albumen for $H_20$ (90%), protein (10%), shock absorption
- shell for protection ($CaCO_3$), gas exchange
 
\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/egg.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Yolk investment varies with maturity at birth 

- **precocial**: capable of moving and feeding itself soon after hatching  
- **altricial**: hatched helpless; requiring significant parental care  

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/yolk_pr_al.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Sotherland & Rahn 1987)

# Egg production

- Usually 1 egg per day max
- **Determinate layers**: lay a fixed total of eggs per nesting attempt
- **Indeterminate layers**: try for a set number of eggs in nest

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6}

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Data from Table 2B
data <- tribble(
  ~Development, ~Laying_type, ~Count,
  "Precocial", "Determinate", 9,
  "Precocial", "Removal", 10,
  "Precocial", "Addition", 2,
  "Precocial", "Removal + Addition", 2,
  "Altricial", "Determinate", 15,
  "Altricial", "Removal", 4,
  "Altricial", "Addition", 2,
  "Altricial", "Removal + Addition", 2
)

# Convert to proportions within each developmental category
data_prop <- data %>%
  group_by(Development) %>%
  mutate(Proportion = Count / sum(Count))

# Factor order for consistent display
data_prop$Laying_type <- factor(data_prop$Laying_type,
                                levels = c("Determinate", "Removal", "Addition", "Removal + Addition"))

# Plot proportions
ggplot(data_prop, aes(x = Laying_type, y = Proportion, fill = Development)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "Laying type",
    y = "Proportion of species"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4575b4", "#d73027")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1)
  )

```

\hfill \tiny ("addition" and "removal" indicate eggs were added or taken away to show indeterminancy; data from Kennedy 1991)

# Why might more precocial species be indeterminate layers?

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6}

  "Precocial", "Determinate", 9,
  "Precocial", "Removal", 10,
  "Precocial", "Addition", 2,
  "Precocial", "Removal + Addition", 2,
  "Altricial", "Determinate", 15,
  "Altricial", "Removal", 4,
  "Altricial", "Addition", 2,
  "Altricial", "Removal + Addition", 2
)

# Convert to proportions within each developmental category
data_prop <- data %>%
  group_by(Development) %>%
  mutate(Proportion = Count / sum(Count))

# Factor order for consistent display

                                levels = c("Determinate", "Removal", "Addition", "Removal + Addition"))

# Plot proportions
ggplot(data_prop, aes(x = Laying_type, y = Proportion, fill = Development)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "Laying type",
    y = "Proportion of species"

    legend.position = "right",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1)
```

# Egg pigmentation

- Egg color and pattern varies widely
- $H$: Trade-off between protection from **transmittance** (T) of UV radiation and **absorption** (A) and overheating. (Dashed line total fitness)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/egg_color.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Lahti & Ardia 2016)  

# Sex ratio adjustment in birds

- Female birds can adjust which sex chromosome the eggs receive in response to the social and/or environmental conditions!
- Theory predicts females will produce more males to maximize their own fitness in species with high variance in male reproductive success---evidence from kakapo below:

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6}

# Load libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)  # to arrange plots side by side

# Data extracted from the table
kakapo <- data.frame(
  Feeding = c(rep("Supplementary fed", 10),
              rep("Not supplementary fed", 8)),
  Proportion_males = c(
    1, 1, 0.67, 1, 0.5, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0.5,     # Supplementary fed
    0.33, 0, 0, 0.5, 0, 1, 0, 0.5            # Not supplementary fed
  ),
  Clutch_size = c(
    3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2,             # Supplementary fed
    3, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2                     # Not supplementary fed
  )
)

# Summarize means and SEs
summary_data <- kakapo %>%
  group_by(Feeding) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_prop = mean(Proportion_males),
    se_prop = sd(Proportion_males) / sqrt(n()),
    mean_clutch = mean(Clutch_size),
    se_clutch = sd(Clutch_size) / sqrt(n())
  )

# Plot 1: Proportion males
p1 <- ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = Feeding, y = mean_prop, fill = Feeding)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_prop - se_prop, ymax = mean_prop + se_prop),
                width = 0.2) +
  labs(y = "Mean proportion males", x = NULL,
       title = "Sex ratio by feeding treatment") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Plot 2: Clutch size
p2 <- ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = Feeding, y = mean_clutch, fill = Feeding)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_clutch - se_clutch, ymax = mean_clutch + se_clutch),
                width = 0.2) +
  labs(y = "Mean clutch size", x = NULL,
       title = "Clutch size by feeding treatment") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Combine side-by-side
p1 + p2

```

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QzqGuFWE2Gs

\hfill \tiny(data from Clout et al. 2002)

# Adjusting hatching order reduces mortality

- House Finches in Montana (**A**) and Alabama (**B**) are diverging in tarsus length; hatching order has impacts on growth rate
- By sex-biasing hatching order, females can reduce mortality in offspring (**D**) by matching tarsus length to local environment

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width =  0.5\linewidth]{images/hatching_order.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Badyaev et al. 2002)  

# Is $H_1$ supported?

- **Clutch size** is number of eggs per nesting attempt
- $H_1$: Clutch size determined by available resources in breeding season (or morality via seasonality leading to greater investment, or lower population density...)
- Prediction: larger clutch sizes at high latitudes

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/clutch_size.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Jetz et al. 2008)  

\normalsize

a) yes
b) no
c) it depends
